open_obligations: Note that no RL agent is trained, so learning speed with sparse reward is not measured.
Check that synthetic labels from PRMlarge are a fair stand-in for expensive human labels.
Check the reported underperformance at 200 samples per problem before extrapolating the 2.6x figure.
out.other_title: Proposed experiments: can RL learn nearly as fast with reward on 10% of episodes?
out.rationale: Amodei et al. propose actively requested reward samples as a step for semi-supervised RL. Lightman et al. estimate that active learning on convincing wrong-answer solutions is about 2.6x more data efficient than uniform labelling when training process reward models; the supervision is synthetic (from a large PRM), the learner is a reward model, and no RL agent is trained.
out.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: whether actively choosing which samples get expensive supervision improves data efficiency, for reward samples in Atari RL (an experiment Amodei et al. propose) versus labels for training process reward models (Lightman et al.)

text: By comparing slopes of best-fit lines with and without active learning, the authors estimate that active learning (training on samples scored by PRMlarge, of which 80% are the most convincing wrong-answer samples according to PRMselector and 20% are the most convincing remaining right- or wrong-answer samples) is approximately 2.6x more data efficient than uniform data labelling; the model trained on the largest active learning dataset (200 samples per problem) appears to slightly underperform the expected trend line.
title: Active learning on convincing wrong-answer solutions gives ~2.6x data efficiency
